texts.preamble: Janga Rajeshwari, vs The State Of Telangana, on 15 June, 2023 Bench: K.Lakshman, P.Sree Sudha Hon'Ble Sri Justice K. Lakshman And Hon'Ble Smt. Justice P. Sree Sudha Writ Petition No.7680 Of 2023 Common Order:
texts.facts: 2. This Writ Petition is filed to issue a writ of Habeas Corpus directing the 3rd respondent to produce the detenu i.e., Janga Venkanna now detained in Central Prison Chanchalguda, Hyderabad and [LEAKAGE_MASK] the impugned detention order passed by the 2nd respondent vide SB.ID.No.138/S1/PD-KMM/2022 dated 28.12.2022 and consequential Confirmation order, if any passed by 1st respondent as illegal. 3. Perusal of the record would reveal that five cases were registered against the detenu. In all these cases, the allegations against the detenu are that he is committing theft by breaking open house and looting. Therefore, according to respondent No.2, detention order was KL,J & PSS,J passed to prevent the detenu in committing similar offences and on consideration of entire material. Therefore, the detenu is a habitual offender and to prevent him for committing similar offences, detention order was passed as per Section 3 of the Telangana Prevention of Dangerous Activites of Boot-Leggers, Dacoits, Drug-Offenders, Goondas, Immoral Traffic Offenders, Land-Grabbers, Spurious Seed Offenders, Insecticide Offenders, Fertiliser Offenders, Food Adulteration Offenders, Fake Document Offenders, Scheduled Commodities Offenders, Forest Document Offenders, Scheduled Commodities Offenders, Forest Offenders, Gaming Offenders, Sexual Offenders, Explosive Substances Offenders, Arms Offenders, Cyber Crime Offenders and White Collar or Financial Offenders Act, 1986. Respondent No.2 has considered the entire material on record and also nature and manner of offences committed by the detenu. Therefore, according to learned Special Government Pleader, there is no error in the detention order. He further submits that the 1st respondent considered the report submitted by the Advisory Board considering the entire material and also nature and manner of offences committed by the detenu. Therefore, there is no irregularity in confirming the detention order by the 1st respondent vide G.O.Rt.No.270 dated 17.02.2023. KL,J & PSS,J 4.
texts.arguments: Whereas, learned counsel appearing for petitioner would submit that respondents have not filed any application seeking cancellation of bail in subsequent crimes registered against the detenu on the ground that detenu herein has committed similar offences in violation of conditions of bail Janga Rajeshwari, vs The State Of Telangana, on 15 June, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/21636116/ 1 imposed by the Court below in the 1st crime. Without taking such steps, respondent No.2 has passed impugned detention order. 5. In Ashok Kumar v. Delhi Administration1, Apex Court observed that preventive detention is devised to afford protection to society. The object is not to punish a man for having done something but to intercept before he does it and to prevent him from doing. 6. In Sushanta Kumar Banik v. State of Tripura2, the Apex Court held that the preventive detention is a serious invasion of personal liberty and the normal methods open to a person charged with commission of any offence to disprove the charge or to prove his innocence at the trial are not available to the person preventively detained and, therefore, in prevention detention jurisprudence, whatever little safeguards the Constitution and the enactments . 7. In Ram Manohar Lohia v. State of Bihar3, the Apex Court held as under: "...Does the expression "public order" take in every kind of disorder or only some? The answer to this serves to distinguish "public order" from "law and order" because the latter undoubtedly takes in all of them. Public order if disturbed, must lead to public disorder. Every breach of the peace does not lead to public disorder. When two drunkards quarrel and fight there is disorder but not public disorder. They can be dealt with under the powers to maintain law and order but cannot be detained on the ground that they were disturbing public order. Suppose that the two fighters were of rival communities and one of them tried to raise communal passions. The problem is still one of law and order but it raises the apprehension of public disorder. The contravention of law always affects order but before it can be said to affect public order, it must affect the community or the public at large. A mere disturbance of law and order leading to disorder is thus not necessarily sufficient for action under the Defence of India Act but disturbances which subvert the public order are. (1966) 1 SCR 709 KL,J & PSS,J affecting "security of State", "law and order" also comprehends disorders of less gravity than those affecting public order". One has to imagine three concentric circles. It is then easy to see that an act may affect law and order but not public order just as an act may affect public order but not security of the State." 8. Janga Rajeshwari, vs The State Of Telangana, on 15 June, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/21636116/ 2 9. In VASANTHU SUMALATHA v. STATE OF ANDHRA PRAESH4 it was held that as there is no reference therein to the orders passed by Courts granting conditional bail to the detenu, the detention orders are vitiated by non-consideration of vital and relevant material. In another judgment dated 11.06.2020 in W.P.No.4125 of 2020 in Shabana Begum vs. State of Telangana5 it was held that one of the essential requirements for passing an order of detention is that ordinary criminal law is not deterrent upon the detenu and thus, preventive detention law needs to be invoked.
